content:
A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence in a trade secrets case. Just days after, Apple fired back, similarly accusing OpenAI of exceeding what court rules allow in its response. Here are the details.

Apple pointed out that OpenAI's actions have gone beyond simply opposing the new evidence.

In the lawsuit in which Apple sued two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products for alleged misappropriation of trade secrets, part of the case involves a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In short, Apple asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction, arguing this would stop its trade secrets from being incorporated into OpenAI's hardware development work while the case is being heard.

In the legal back-and-forth over that motion, Apple submitted an opposition brief along with five expert declarations. The defendants then promptly accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence and asked the court to strike portions of the documents.

In the defendants' opposition papers, in addition to accusing Apple of introducing new evidence, OpenAI and the other defendants also submitted multiple documents to rebut Apple's case.

Apple today filed a reply to the above objections, accusing the defendants of going beyond simply opposing new evidence and instead raising new arguments and evidence of their own:

Under Rule 7-3(d)(1) of the Civil Procedure Rules, a party may oppose new evidence in an opposition brief, but the rule also makes clear that the document "shall not present further arguments on the motion itself." The defendants did not follow this rule, however, and instead used their document to re-litigate the substance of the preliminary injunction motion. For example, the defendants disputed whether Dr. Runge has "a sufficient basis for analysis," whether he adequately addressed "rebuttal evidence," and whether he proved that certain Apple materials are not publicly available. ⋯⋯ This kind of argument is not an opposition to new evidence. ⋯⋯ (Statements that "the plaintiff's position lacks evidentiary support or is weakened by other evidence" do not constitute "opposition to evidence.")

Apple also challenged a new declaration submitted by Liu, calling it "the most serious overreach" in the defendants' papers:

Notably, when submitting his declaration, the defendants stated that the court should consider it only together with the Apple evidence being challenged.

Apple pointed out, however, that since the defendants have introduced new arguments of their own, the court should consider the full record rather than striking any evidence Apple raised in its opposition brief.

The court has scheduled the preliminary injunction hearing for October 14.
